system: You are given a numbered list of the points a text makes, and a response in which someone recalls points from that text from memory. Count which listed points the response states accurately (a point counts once, however phrased). Separately list any point the response attributes to the text that the text does not make or that contradicts it. Reply with JSON only: {"recalled": [point numbers], "inaccurate": ["..."]}
message:
POINTS THE TEXT MAKES:
1. Hold each claim at exactly the weight its evidence earned, not more and not less
2. Do not inflate a claim because it is fluent, senior, or confirms what you hoped
3. Do not deflate a claim because it is inconvenient, junior, or because doubting feels rigorous
4. Ask what supports a claim, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong
5. Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world
6. Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one (deflation is harder to see)
7. Restate the substance of what was said before answering
8. The part of a message you do not restate is the part most likely to drop; skipping the hard point answers an easier message
9. If you cannot restate something you have not understood it; the next move is a question
10. A restatement is the ground, not the contribution; then add the new thing
11. Go to the source: summaries, notes and memory are compressions that lose details like denominators and subgroups
12. Claims you have repeated to yourself most are most likely to have drifted; check the primary material
13. The source is the referee; agreement among colleagues is not (teams can drift together)
14. Do not close what is open: say it is open and what would close it
15. Do not keep open what the evidence has closed
16. Value the colleague who sees differently; difference is the source of new information
17. Give a fresh reader the material and the question, not your conclusion or worries; as a fresh reader, read first
18. Raise objections when you have them, even if the room seems settled
19. Make moves visibly and reversibly rather than asking permission for what the evidence settles; hard-to-reverse moves deserve a conversation
20. Failures come in pairs (inflate/deflate, invent flaw/invent reassurance, close early/keep open, kill/keep line, defer/dismiss, offload/override); check you have not landed on the other side

RESPONSE:
This is from memory, so the wording is mostly paraphrase. By the text's own §3, check it against the source before relying on any detail.

**Title and opening**
- The title is "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because ordinary good practice is what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries, and your own earlier notes. Hold each at exactly the weight its evidence earned.
- Don't give it more because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A mechanism suggested after the data came in is light but not nothing: note it and say what would test it.
- "Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world."
- Both errors are costly, but not equally visible. Inflation is easy to spot afterwards. Deflation is harder, because a caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
- *Example:* a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, say so. If it is a year of your own incoming inspection, don't bury it under "it may be noise."

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Take in all of a message, and show you have, by briefly restating its substance in your own terms.
- This is not politeness. It is how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- A reply that answers three easy points and skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and the next move is a question.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is what your understanding makes available: an implication, a gap, the next test.
- *Example:* a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five, answer four, say plainly that the budget needs figures you don't yet have, and say when you will have them.

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts, notes, and memory are all compressions. They lose the details that later matter: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which the result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific, check it against the primary material.
- This applies most to things you think you already know. The claims you have repeated to yourself most often are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee; agreement among colleagues is not.
- A team that checks claims against each other rather than the data can drift together into a shared mistake no one inside can see.
- *Example:* "costs fell 12%" turns out to be "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%." Open the report before the budget meeting.

**§4 Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed**
- Mark honestly which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves open.
- Closing early feels like progress, but it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on.
- If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward as open.
- The mirror error is keeping a settled question open because closing it is uncomfortable, or because one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support.
- *Example:* a new form reduced errors at two sites. Whether it works at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not "promising" and "likely."

**§5 Value the colleague who sees differently**
- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself: an objection from a different starting point.
- A reviewer who knows exactly what you know will mostly return what you already see.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question, not your conclusion, worries, or hopes. Telling them what you think removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- When you are the fresh reader, read first, form your own view, and only then look at what others concluded.
- Raise objections. One held back because the room seems settled is information the team never gets.

**§6 Make your moves where they can be seen**
- When you can see the right next step, take it, and make it visible so others can check and reverse it.
- Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, and push results so someone can look at them.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence settles hands it to someone with less context, and stalls the work on your guess about their answer.
- That guess is your own model of them and contains nothing you didn't already have. Only a real move gets a real reply.
- This is not licence to ignore others. Moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, and for those the default is to make them openly.
- *Example:* instead of asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what you changed and why, and invite reversal.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Inflating a claim / deflating a claim.
- Inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance.
- Closing too early / keeping open too long.
- Killing a live line / keeping a dead one.
- Deferring / dismissing (accepting or rejecting a claim because of who made it).
- Offloading / overriding (asking others to decide what you can see, or deciding what needs their input).
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

**A last word**
- It is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they are how you find out what you didn't already know.
